title: Variables & Types
description: Learn about variables, types, and type conversions in Go
theory:
## Variables in Go

In Go, variables are declared using the `var` keyword or using the short declaration operator `:=`.

### Variable Declaration

The basic syntax is:
```go
var name string = "Alice"
var age int = 25
```

Or using short declaration (only inside functions):
```go
name := "Alice"
age := 25
```

### Basic Types

Go has several basic types:
- **Integers**: `int`, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64` (signed) and `uint`, `uint8`, `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64` (unsigned)
- **Floating Point**: `float32`, `float64`
- **Complex**: `complex64`, `complex128`
- **String**: `string`
- **Boolean**: `bool`


### Type Inference

When you assign a value at declaration, Go infers the type:
```go
x := 10      // int
y := 10.5    // float64
name := "hi" // string
```

### Zero Values

Variables declared without initialization get a zero value:
- `0` for numeric types
- `""` for strings
- `false` for booleans
- `nil` for pointers, interfaces, slices, maps, channels, functions


### Type Conversions

Go is a statically typed language. You must explicitly convert between types:
```go
var i int = 42
var f float64 = float64(i)
var u uint = uint(i)
```

### Constants

Constants are declared with `const` and cannot be changed:
```go
const Pi = 3.14159
const Name = "Go" // untyped constant
```

exercises.title: Declare a Variable
exercises.description: Declare a variable age of type int and assign it the value 25. Then use fmt.Println to print it.
hints: Use var age int = 25 or age := 25 to declare and assign

exercises.title: Multiple Variable Declaration
exercises.description: Declare two variables: name (string) with value "Golang" and version (float64) with value 1.21. Print them on the same line separated by a space.
hints: Use var name string = "Golang" or name := "Golang"
Use var version float64 = 1.21 or version := 1.21
exercises.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    name := "Golang"
    version := 1.21
    fmt.Println(name, version)
}

exercises.title: Type Conversion
exercises.description: Declare an integer variable x with value 100. Convert it to a float64 and store in y. Print the result.
hints: Use float64(x) to convert int to float64
exercises.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    x := 100
    y := float64(x)
    fmt.Println(y)
}

exercises.title: Zero Values
exercises.description: Declare variables of type int, float64, string, and bool without assigning values. Print each one to see their zero values.
hints: var intVar int declares an int with zero value 0
var strVar string has zero value "" (empty string)
var boolVar bool has zero value false
exercises.solution:
package main

import "fmt"


func main() {
    var intVar int
    var floatVar float64
    var strVar string
    var boolVar bool
    fmt.Println(intVar, floatVar, strVar, boolVar)
}

exercises.title: Constants
exercises.description: Create a constant named MaxScore with value 100 and a constant named MinScore with value 0. Print both constants.
hints: Use const MaxScore = 100 (Go infers the type)
exercises.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    const MaxScore = 100
    const MinScore = 0
    fmt.Println(MaxScore, MinScore)
}

exercises.title: Grouped Variable Declaration
exercises.description: Use a grouped var declaration to declare host (string, "localhost"), port (int, 8080), and debug (bool, true). Print all three values.
hints: Use var ( host string = "localhost"; port int = 8080; debug bool = true )

exercises.title: Variable Swap
exercises.description: Declare two variables a and b with values 5 and 10. Swap their values without using a temp variable. Print the values after swapping.
hints: In Go, you can swap in one line: a, b = b, a
exercises.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    a, b := 5, 10
    a, b = b, a
    fmt.Println(a, b)
}
